At Oyama in Shimotsuke, Toshizō heard a curious scouting report.
(Well, well — it seems there is such a thing as fate in the affairs of men.)
His fight in the eastern outskirts of the town over, Toshizō was walking slowly up the town's central road toward the honjin where the commander-in-chief, Ōtori Keisuke, was.
The Imperial force in Utsunomiya Castle, seven ri to the north of here, was, it seemed, that same corps which had taken Kondō at Nagareyama.
The commanders were the Satsuma man Arima Tōta and the Mito man Kagawa Keizō.
Against these two he had a grudge.
Three hundred men.
(Shall I make a meal of them?)
He thought to take his revenge fair and square in the open field.
For one thing, even this quarrel-loving man had never yet led an army to attack a castle.
Treading the blackish earth of Oyama post-town, Toshizō could not master the excitement welling up in him.
He reached the honjin. He went up into it still in his straw sandals.
Ōtori too sat cross-legged, still sandal-shod, in an inner room.
White-faced, he was poring over a map. He did not even notice Toshizō come in.
Ōtori was, among the former shogunal men, the foremost authority on things Western, and his knowledge of military science was highly prized.
But it was all knowledge out of translations; in the ability to fight a real battle he was an unknown quantity.

A brilliant scholar, of course. And because he was a brilliant, learned man, he was overrated as having the gifts of a general. In truth he had no talent for command. With the instinct of a born brawler, Toshizō saw through it.
──What now? What was he to do?
So Ōtori sat at his wits' end. True, in the small skirmishes so far it had been victory upon victory; but after this, what should he do?
"Ōtori,"
Toshizō stood looking down at him.
He raised his eyes with a start.
"It's me,"
Not the enemy.
Ōtori flushed. But at once a look of displeasure came over him at Toshizō's intrusion.
"What do you want?"
said Ōtori, with pointed politeness.
"Next we should attack Utsunomiya Castle,"
Toshizō pronounced, as if he had seen clean through Ōtori's irresolution.
"Utsunomiya Castle?"

Ōtori's face said: absurd. It was a great and famous castle. In the terms of Western military art this would be a siege of a fortress, and in the West a fortress-siege was undertaken with preparations a Japanese would think excessive.
"It can't be done,"
he said with a pitying smile. What could this boss of the Shinsengumi understand, was the thought behind it.
Toshizō, for his part, saw plainly the feeling behind this Western-studies pedant's words.
But Toshizō had his pride: that he had been tempered through and through amid flashing blades and hails of shot.
(War needs no book-learning. Had any of the great captains of old their learning? A general's capacity and gift are not got by study; they are inborn. And I have them.)
Toshizō did feel an inferiority before Ōtori's learning, and just for that his pride in his own powers grew the stronger.
"Can't be done?"
said Toshizō.
"Then where do you attack next?"
"Here,"
and Ōtori jabbed a finger at a point on the map just two and a half ri northwest of Oyama. That place was —
Mibu.

At Mibu was a small walled castle some three chō to a side, the seat of Torii Tango-no-kami's thirty thousand koku. A small Imperial force had already entered it; but it was so slight a castle that it could surely be crushed with a single twist.
"We pass through this Mibu. If they open on us we fight; if not, we go straight on to Nikkō,"
The final objective of going to Nikkō had already been settled in the council of war.

Toshizō held it a good plan. Make the Nikkō Tōshōgū a fortress, entrench in the north Kantō upon the natural fastness of the Nikkō massif, and the Imperial army could not easily attack. While they harried it there, the lords of the realm discontented with Satsuma and Chōshū would surely rise together. This army meant to play the strategic part that Kusunoki Masashige had played in the Kenmu Restoration. Nikkō would become the Tokugawa's Chihaya castle.
"Well, Mibu can pass. But to leave Utsunomiya Castle be will sow the seed of trouble for the future, mark you,"
Toshizō went on:

"Utsunomiya is what the art of war calls a focal ground. The Ōu highway, the Nikkō Reiheishi highway, and many roads besides gather here and run out from here. On another day, when the Imperial army comes to attack Nikkō, it will pack a great force into this Utsunomiya and send its troops out from it. This castle we must take and hold,"
"You say it lightly,"
said Ōtori, tapping the map with his pencil,
"but suppose by some chance we do take the castle. To hold a castle of that size wants a thousand men. When I think of the holding of it, I have no wish to lay a finger on Utsunomiya,"
"No matter — we have only to seize it. Word that the great bastion of the north Kantō had fallen would tell heavily on the lords now sitting on the fence,"
"I will not take it,"
"I see,"
Toshizō gave a wry smile. He had foreseen this answer from the first.
"Then lend me three hundred men and the two guns we've just captured,"
said Toshizō.
"You mean to say you can take it with no more than that?"
"I can take it,"
The sun was already going down, but Toshizō set out at once.
For his men he put the little Western-trained Kuwana troops in the van, with part of the Denshūtai and the Kaitentai following.
His second was the Aizu retainer Akizuki Tonosuke.

Marching by night, they were billeted in the houses along the highway, and the next day camped at Tadenuma on the east bank of the Kinugawa, four ri from the town below Utsunomiya Castle, making this their staging-ground for the attack.
"Akizuki, do you know Utsunomiya?"
said Toshizō.
Akizuki, being an Aizu retainer, held the former vice-commander of the Shinsengumi in deep respect.
"I've been there, but I hardly went with any thought of attacking the castle-town of Toda Tosa-no-kami, worth 77,000 koku, so I don't remember it well,"
Toshizō, for once, laughed too, and,
"I know it only from the storytellers' tale of the Utsunomiya hanging ceiling,"
he said.
Toshizō had the local people brought to him, built up as detailed a map as he could, and questioned them carefully about the castle's moats, the lay of the surrounding ground, the streets.
"This place — attack from the southeast of the castle and it'll fall,"
he muttered under his breath.
Utsunomiya Castle, on the side of its main gate, had deep moats and cunningly contrived fields of fire from its turrets, and was formidable enough; but in Toshizō's phrase,
"its flank was no good,"

— meaning the southeastern part of the castle. Here were many copses and bamboo thickets, easy to screen one from the castle's fire; and on this side the embankment was low and the moat-water dried bone-dry.
"Against the main gate we'll send just enough men to draw the enemy's eye, and the main body will come by a byway and attack from this wooded ground,"
Before dawn the next day he set the force in motion.
On horseback, Toshizō —
(Kondō, they say, has been taken to the Itabashi headquarters — but is he truly safe?)
the thought would not leave his mind.
At all events, the enemy of Shimōsa Nagareyama now held Utsunomiya Castle in Shimotsuke.
Wipe them out and take prisoners, and he might somehow learn news of him.
In the castle, the Satsuma man Arima Tōta and the Mito man Kagawa Keizō were now elated, now cast down, at the reports of mounted scouts and spies galloping back from every quarter.
The reports were, every one, of the movements of the main body under Ōtori Keisuke, which had come from Oyama through Iizuka and was advancing on the castle-town of Mibu.
That Toshizō's little detachment was beginning to show its head at Tadenuma to the southwest, they never suspected.
"the Edo break-out corps,"
— so they called Ōtori's army.
"The break-out corps most likely means to avoid Utsunomiya, take the byways out to Kanuma, and go on to Nikkō from there,"
— so both Arima and Kagawa judged.
"In that case there's nothing for it but to let them pass in peace,"
Arima had given up any thought of sallying out to fight.

For the Imperial troops in Utsunomiya Castle, though their commander was the Satsuma man Arima Tōta, were no picked men of Satsuma, Chōshū, and Tosa, but three hundred old-equipped Hikone domain soldiers who would lose if it came to a fight.
This Arima force was a mere detachment. Their parent body, the Imperial Tōsandō force, still lay unmoving with its headquarters at Itabashi.
"The break-out corps's captain is apparently Ōtori Keisuke,"

— such was the rumor that had reached them. The shogunal army's foremost authority on the Western-style land forces, and the greater part of his runaways were Western-drilled infantry. The Hikone troops in Arima's charge could not hope to beat them.
"Times have changed,"
said Arima Tōta.
The house of Ii of Hikone, in Ieyasu's day,
the Red Regiment of Ii,

was famed throughout the land for its might. Ieyasu's Tokugawa host, by settled rule after Sekigahara, took the Ii, first among the hereditary vassals, and the Tōdō, of the outer lords, for its vanguard; and in the winter and summer campaigns at Osaka these two forces served, in fact, as the drill-bit at the point of the van.

Ieyasu had labored to make the Ii the strongest of his corps, taking many masterless men of the Takeda house of Kai into service and attaching them to it. The Red Regiment of Takeda had become, just so, the Red Regiment of Ii.
But the age of sword and spear was past.
The Hikone domain was now, of all the domains, about the weakest fighting force there was.
"In the old shogunate, say what you like, the strongest now must be the townsman-and-peasant infantry Ōtori leads, and the Denshūtai and the Shōhōtai,"
"It isn't only strong and weak, the change of the age —"
Kagawa gave a little shrug,
"Hikone, called first of the Tokugawa hereditary vassals, has cast off the house of Tokugawa, turned Imperial, and means to fight the old shogunal army,"
he said. For some reason Kagawa bore the Hikone men no goodwill.
The Satsuma man Arima disliked this sharp-tongued streak in Kagawa.
By that reasoning, was not Kagawa himself a man who had belonged to the house of Mito, one of the Three Houses of the Tokugawa?
Meanwhile, to Ōtori, leading the main body, came an envoy from the Mibu domain, who delivered this message:

──Imperial troops have entered this castle of ours. Should you pass through the castle-town, a fight is certain, and we, a house of Tokugawa hereditary vassals, would be caught in the middle, at a loss which way to turn. And if the town becomes a battlefield the common folk will suffer; so if you are bound for Nikkō, will you not go by way of Tochigi? We will furnish guides.

Such was the message, and Ōtori followed it, going round by Tochigi and marching north over bad roads toward Kanuma. From Tochigi to Kanuma is five and a half ri, from Kanuma to Nikkō a little over six.
In Utsunomiya Castle, seeing this movement of Ōtori's force,
"So they've steered clear of our castle,"
Kagawa rejoiced, all but clapping his hands.
This was the nineteenth of the fourth month.
But that afternoon three hundred light troops hauling gun-carriages appeared suddenly to the southeast of the castle, throwing Arima and Kagawa into confusion.
Arima at once sent a platoon of Hikone men out to the east of the castle.
Toshizō was at the head of that surprise force.
The moment the Hikone men showed on the plain east of the castle, he had his own men fan out and rush forward, firing as they went.
Toshizō sat his horse unruffled. At his horse's side fluttered a corps-banner inscribed in bold characters, "Tōshō-Daigongen."
"Get down, sir, get down,"
Akizuki called out again and again, keeping himself low against the paddy-bank.
Toshizō smiled and shook his head. He had a faith that no bullet would strike him.
And in fact the bullets seemed to fly wide of Toshizō.
The men, running from cover to cover, firing and running, firing and running, closed in.
The distance between the two sides came down to fifty ken.
Toshizō, from the saddle,
"Cease fire. Charge,"
he shouted. In a rush the Kuwana men and the Denshū and Kaiten units broke into a run.
Toshizō galloped at their head, but partway his horse was shot through the muzzle and went down.
In the same instant he leapt clear and drove in among the Hikone men as they tried to fall back.
He cut them down.
Laid about him, one might say. Presently his own men came charging in in a mass.
The enemy fled.
Pursuing them, he pushed into the dense copse and bamboo southeast of the castle, had the gun set up there, and opened fire on the castle's east gate.
"Smash the gate-doors,"
said Toshizō.
Three rounds were fired. The third struck the east gate, shattered the doors, and burst.

Meanwhile he sent part of the Kuwana men running to set fires here and there in the castle-town, had the Denshūtai fire from full in front of the main gate, and himself, leading the main body, leapt down into the dry moat, ran under the bullets in one dash, and gained the front of the east gate.
Utsunomiya Castle, be it noted, out of deference to the shogunate on account of the famous Utsunomiya affair of the early Tokugawa years, had within its walls no buildings to speak of.
In the end, once the gate's defense was broken, the fighting within the walls was easy.
"Charge the gate, charge it,"
Toshizō roared.
Hikone men swarmed at the gate-side, firing their old-model Gewehr muskets.
His own side, firing back with Minié rifles, pressed on.
At last friend and foe were ten paces apart, and for some minutes, at just that distance, the two sides fired fiercely at each other.
Toshizō grew exasperated.
In the Shinsengumi's brilliant days, they would never have come this close and then stood each nursing the distance between them.
At Toshizō's side were Saitō Hajime, once a jokin serving under the vice-commander of the Shinsengumi, and six others of the old comrades.
"Rifles, stop, the rifles —"
he bawled at his own men, making them cease fire, and,
"Shinsengumi, forward!"
he yelled, and charged in through the gate.
Saitō Hajime slipped past Toshizō at a run, closed inside the reach of a Hikone man who came at him with a leveled spear, and clove him clean in two with a stroke from overhead.
As the blood sprang up in a spray, Toshizō's Izumi-no-kami Kanesada was already tracing an arc and splitting from the crown of the skull a man who had darted out behind him.
──The Shinsengumi are here!
The Hikone men shuddered with dread.
In a rush they fled back inside the gate.
Just then a round from Toshizō's gunners, firing from the thin wood behind, struck the powder magazine within the castle.
A small fire started. Presently, with a great roar, it blew up.
Toshizō and his men ranged through the castle.
"Find the Imperial staff officers, the staff officers,"

Toshizō shouted it, drenched head to foot in the blood of his kills. Take them and avenge Nagareyama; learn whether Kondō was alive or dead — this assault on the castle had, for Toshizō, only those two aims.
Toshizō searched all through the enclosure. Now and then a castle soldier too slow to escape sprang out and struck at him, but each time it ended in a cruel result.
None of them knew that this man in Western battle-dress was Hijikata Toshizō, once vice-commander of the Shinsengumi.
The fighting within the walls did not stop even at sundown.
The enemy too fought stubbornly.
Toshizō, a torch held high in his left hand and a great sword in his right, sought out the enemy.
After eight in the evening the enemy, leaving their dead behind in the enclosure, fell back northward out of it, meaning to rally at a temple on Myōjin-yama to the north of the castle.
As the enemy's retreat began, Toshizō, leading his old Shinsengumi comrades, drove straight into the mass of the retreating men's torches.
From among the retreating men twenty or thirty shots cracked out, and bullets came flying, cutting the night air.
Still he charged on.
Just then a fearsome battle-cry broke out right under Toshizō's nose.
He dodged.
He cut down.
There was, for certain, the feel of a hit. But the enemy shape did not fall, and slipped away as it was into the fleeing men.
That, it seems, had been Arima Tōta.
Toshizō's blade appears to have slashed open the muscle of Arima's chest.
But it only grazed him. Arima kept his life, was borne off and treated at the hospital in Yokohama, and afterward recovered.
Ōtori, the next day, had pushed forward to Kanuma, three ri west of Utsunomiya, and, seeing the smoke of fire rising over the castle far off, knew that it had fallen.
(That man —)
And in secret he marveled.
